articles.title: CRISPR could help doctors attack blood cancer without destroying healthy cells
articles.summary: Researchers used CRISPR to remove CD33 from donor stem cells, potentially giving doctors a way to attack aggressive blood cancers without destroying the healthy cells patients need after a transplant. In a 30-patient trial, the edited cells successfully took hold and appeared to shield blood cells from a CD33-targeted cancer treatment.
articles.content:
For some of the most aggressive blood cancers, a stem cell transplant may be the only treatment with the potential to cure the disease. Even so, cancers can return after transplantation, leaving doctors with limited options.

A new clinical trial led by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis suggests that genetically modifying donor stem cells before transplantation could make follow-up cancer treatments safer and potentially more effective. The strategy removes a specific protein from donor cells so that therapies aimed at that protein can attack cancer while sparing healthy transplanted cells.

The study was conducted at Siteman Cancer Center, based at Barnes-Jewish Hospital and WashU Medicine, and 14 other sites in the U.S. and Canada. The results were published in Nature Medicine.

A Major Challenge for CAR-T Therapy

According to corresponding author John F. DiPersio, MD, PhD, the Virginia E. & Sam J. Golman Professor of Medicine at WashU Medicine, the gene editing approach could help overcome a major obstacle that has limited CAR-T cell therapy in certain blood cancers.

CAR-T therapy has proved highly effective against some aggressive blood cancers, but it has not worked as well against diseases such as acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS).

The problem, DiPersio explained, is that many proteins found on AML and MDS cancer cells also appear on healthy myeloid cells, including donor stem cells used in transplantation. If CAR-T cells are programmed to attack one of those shared proteins, they may destroy healthy blood stem cells along with the cancer.

That damage can trigger a dangerous inflammatory response. It may also weaken the cancer treatment itself because large numbers of CAR-T cells end up attacking healthy targets instead of concentrating on malignant cells.

The underlying idea for avoiding this problem was first described by Miriam Y. Kim, MD, now an assistant professor of medicine at WashU Medicine. Kim began the research as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Pennsylvania and continued it in the DiPersio lab before becoming an independent investigator in the WashU Medicine Division of Oncology. She treats patients at Siteman and is also a research member there.

Removing CD33 From Healthy Stem Cells

In the clinical trial, patients with AML and MDS received donor stem cells that had been genetically modified to remove a protein called CD33. The goal was to create healthy blood cells that would no longer be vulnerable to treatments designed to attack CD33.

"We are encouraged by the results of this study showing that a CD33-deleted stem cell transplant looks very similar to the outcomes of standard stem cell transplantation," said DiPersio, who also directs WashU Medicine's Center for Gene and Cellular Immunotherapy. "In the future, we are hopeful we will be able to combine this with CD33-targeted immunotherapies, such as CAR-T cells, and improve treatment options for patients with these very aggressive blood cancers."

DiPersio and his collaborators have also reported a single case involving a patient with high-risk AML who received a CD33-deleted stem cell transplant. When the cancer later returned, the patient was treated with CD33-targeted CAR-T cells made from T cells provided by the same donor who supplied the original stem cells.

The patient, who had one of the most aggressive forms of AML, entered complete remission and remained cancer-free more than one year after CAR-T treatment. Normal blood cell production also returned, and all of the patient's blood cells lacked CD33. That finding indicated that the genetically engineered donor cells had successfully established themselves in the bone marrow. DiPersio is the senior author of that study, which was published in October 2025 in JCO Precision Oncology.

Shielding Healthy Blood Cells

CD33 is an attractive target for this strategy because the protein is found only on blood-forming cells and not on other tissues. Evidence also suggests that CD33 is not necessary for normal blood stem cell function, since people born without the protein do not appear to have related health problems.

After a successful transplant with CD33-deleted stem cells, the theory is that any cells still carrying CD33 should primarily be cancer cells. A CAR-T therapy or another immunotherapy targeting CD33 could then attack those cancer cells while leaving the healthy donor-derived blood cells alone.

The phase 1/2 multicenter trial enrolled 30 adults with AML or MDS who were considered at high risk of relapse. Before transplantation, donor stem cells were modified with CRISPR gene editing to remove CD33.

The resulting CD33-deleted stem cell product is called tremtelectogene empogeditemcel (trem-cel). It was developed by Vor Biopharma, which funded the study.

Testing a CD33-Targeted Cancer Treatment

To test whether the edited stem cells could withstand a therapy directed at CD33, patients also received a maintenance treatment after transplantation.

The drug, gemtuzumab ozogamicin, is not a CD33-targeted CAR-T therapy. Instead, it is an engineered antibody that recognizes CD33 and delivers an anti-cancer drug directly to cells carrying the protein.

Gemtuzumab ozogamicin is approved by the Food and Drug Administration for CD33-positive AML and is being tested in clinical trials for CD33-positive MDS. Although the treatment can help prevent relapse, its usefulness is limited by side effects that include liver toxicity and damage to healthy blood cells. Patients can develop dangerously low levels of white blood cells, red blood cells and platelets.

Gene-Edited Cells Successfully Engrafted

All 30 patients achieved engraftment by day 28, meaning the transplanted stem cells reached the bone marrow and began producing blood cells. Some patients reached that milestone sooner, while platelet production returned by day 16, on average.

Those recovery times were similar to what is typically seen with standard stem cell transplantation.

Average survival in the trial was just over 14 months. Nineteen patients received at least one cycle of gemtuzumab ozogamicin as part of a dose-escalation protocol, allowing researchers to identify a recommended dose.

Across the different doses, patients maintained their blood cell counts. The finding suggests that the gene-edited transplant protected them from the severe drops in blood cells that often occur when this maintenance therapy is used after a conventional stem cell transplant.

Side Effects Remained Similar to Standard Transplants

The side effects seen during treatment were broadly similar to those associated with standard stem cell transplantation. They included anemia, low platelet counts, fever, infections and graft-versus-host disease, in which donor cells attack the patient's healthy tissues.

Seven patients died during the study. Four deaths resulted from progression of the cancer, while three were linked to transplant-related complications, including kidney failure, liver toxicity and sepsis.

DiPersio said the findings provide a foundation for future treatments that pair CD33-deleted stem cell transplantation with CD33-targeted immunotherapies. The goal is to allow doctors to attack cancer cells more aggressively without simultaneously destroying the healthy donor cells needed to rebuild the patient's blood system.

This work was supported by Vor Biopharma. Several co-authors were employees of the company when the work was conducted.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant medical breakthrough using CRISPR gene editing to improve treatment for aggressive blood cancers by protecting healthy donor stem cells during transplantation and enabling safer, more effective follow-up therapies. The clinical trial results demonstrate successful engraftment and potential for improved patient outcomes, representing a meaningful advancement with broad implications for cancer treatment.
articles.personality_title: Gene editing helps protect healthy cells in blood cancer treatment
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Some aggressive blood cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are very hard to treat. A common way to fight them is with a stem cell transplant, but cancer often comes back. New treatments called CAR-T therapy can attack cancer cells but may also harm healthy blood cells, causing serious problems.

**What happened** – Researchers at Washington University used a gene-editing tool called CRISPR to remove a protein called CD33 from donor stem cells before transplanting them into patients with AML and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). This change helps protect healthy cells from treatments that target CD33 on cancer cells. In a trial with 30 patients, the edited stem cells successfully grew in the bone marrow and helped patients keep healthy blood cells even when given a CD33-targeted drug.

**Impact** – This approach is important because it could allow doctors to use strong therapies that attack cancer without harming healthy blood cells. Normally, treatments targeting CD33 also damage healthy cells, causing dangerous side effects. By removing CD33 from donor cells, the therapy becomes safer and may work better. One patient who received the edited cells and later a CD33-targeted CAR-T treatment went into complete remission for over a year.

**What's next step** – Researchers plan to combine CD33-deleted stem cell transplants with CD33-targeted immunotherapies like CAR-T cells in future studies. This could improve treatment options for patients with tough blood cancers and reduce the risks of current therapies.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using CRISPR to remove CD33 from donor stem cells helps protect healthy blood cells and may make powerful cancer treatments safer and more effective.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’édition génétique protège les cellules saines dans le traitement du cancer du sang
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Certains cancers du sang agressifs comme la leucémie myéloïde aiguë (LMA) sont difficiles à soigner. Une greffe de cellules souches est souvent utilisée, mais le cancer peut revenir. Les thérapies CAR-T peuvent attaquer les cellules cancéreuses, mais elles peuvent aussi détruire des cellules saines, ce qui est dangereux.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université de Washington ont utilisé un outil appelé CRISPR pour retirer une protéine nommée CD33 des cellules souches des donneurs avant la greffe. Ce changement protège les cellules saines des traitements ciblant CD33 sur les cellules cancéreuses. Dans un essai avec 30 patients, les cellules modifiées ont bien pris dans la moelle osseuse et ont aidé les patients à garder des cellules sanguines saines même après un traitement ciblé.

**Impact** – Cette méthode est importante car elle permettrait d’utiliser des traitements puissants contre le cancer sans abîmer les cellules saines. Habituellement, cibler CD33 endommage aussi les bonnes cellules, causant des effets secondaires graves. En retirant CD33, la thérapie devient plus sûre et plus efficace. **Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent associer les greffes avec les cellules CAR-T ciblant CD33 dans de futures études. Cela pourrait améliorer les traitements pour les cancers du sang difficiles et réduire les risques.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Retirer CD33 des cellules souches donneuses grâce à CRISPR protège les cellules saines et rend les traitements du cancer plus sûrs et efficaces.

articles.title: Virtual green spaces and classical music reduce blood pressure in hospital
articles.summary: Watching a river flow via a virtual-reality headset while listening to classical music seems to quickly bring people's blood pressure down from a dangerously high level in hospital
articles.content:
Watching a river flow via a virtual-reality headset while listening to classical music seems to quickly bring people's blood pressure down from a dangerously high level in hospital

Virtual reality could be a simple way of bringing a patient’s blood pressure down Ground Picture/Shutterstock

Gazing at a flowing river while listening to classical music could lower the blood pressure of people in the emergency room. Luckily, as these landscapes and live orchestras are hard to come by in hospitals, virtual reality and playlists do the job.

Dangerously high blood pressure, known as hypertensive urgency, is common among people in intensive-care settings. Medication can prevent it from causing damage to the eyes, heart and brain. However, relaxation approaches, such as looking at aquarium scenes and listening to classical music, have also shown promise.

Now, Safa Dönmez at the University of Health Sciences in Ankara, Turkey, and his colleagues have combined these two approaches to relaxation. The team recruited 130 adults who arrived in an emergency department with hypertensive urgency. These patients are often anxious, which can make their bodies release stress hormones that tighten blood vessels and further hike up blood pressure, says Dönmez.

Advertisement

The researchers gave all the participants standard medication to reduce blood pressure. Half also viewed a scene of the Columbia River in Canada flowing through a forest via a VR headset while listening to a soothing playlist of classical music from the likes of Debussy, Bach and Mozart. “Overall, the aim was to create a calm, natural and relaxing environment,” says Dönmez.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

Before treatment, the participants’ arterial pressure was about 130 to 138 mmHg, on average. Fifteen minutes after the intervention, it had dropped by about 12mmHG among those who only took medication, compared with about 16 mmHg for those also having the VR and music experience. The results were presented at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris, France.

Verónica Saldaña-Ortiz at the European University in Madrid, Spain, says that seeing such results so quickly is clinically significant. “In an emergency department, even a relatively simple non-pharmacological intervention that helps patients feel calmer during the initial phase of care could be clinically valuable,” she says.

After 30 minutes, the difference had shrunk, and by 60 minutes, the blood pressure readings of the two groups were about the same.

The intervention’s initial positive effect on blood pressure may be related to its impact on anxiety, says Dönmez. Anxiety fell by a greater amount in the VR/music group, according to ratings using a questionnaire called the State Anxiety Inventory.

“The results are consistent with a growing body of work that shows that even virtual nature can help reduce stress, including reductions in blood pressure, in stressful situations,” says Mathew White at the University of Exeter, UK. “Extending this approach to an emergency room setting seems like a wonderful idea, and hopefully results can be replicated and more widely implemented if confirmed.”

The VR and classical music were delivered together, so we cannot determine whether the benefit came from the music, the virtual environment or both, says Saldaña-Ortiz. Dönmez says the team is planning to do larger studies with longer follow-up periods to disentangle this and see whether patients choosing their own music makes a difference.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a meaningful, evidence-based health intervention using virtual reality and classical music to reduce dangerously high blood pressure in emergency room patients. This non-pharmacological approach has broad potential clinical significance and could improve patient care and outcomes in a common and serious medical condition. The study is well-described with clear context, results, and expert commentary.
articles.personality_title: Virtual reality and classical music help lower high blood pressure in hospitals
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – High blood pressure can be dangerous and is common in hospital emergency rooms. Usual treatment includes medicine, but stress and anxiety can make it worse by tightening blood vessels.

**What happened** – Researchers in Turkey tested a new way to help patients with very high blood pressure. They gave 130 emergency room patients medicine, and half of them also watched a peaceful river scene through virtual reality (VR) while listening to classical music. They used music by composers like Bach and Mozart to create a calm feeling.

**Impact** – After 15 minutes, patients who used VR and music had a bigger drop in blood pressure than those who only took medicine. Their anxiety also went down more. This shows that simple, non-drug methods can help patients feel calmer and improve health quickly in stressful situations.

**What's next step** – The researchers want to do bigger studies to find out whether the VR, the music, or both together work best. They also plan to see if letting patients choose their own music helps even more.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Combining virtual nature scenes with classical music can quickly reduce high blood pressure and anxiety in hospital patients alongside medicine.

Leur anxiété a aussi diminué plus fortement. Cela montre que des méthodes simples, sans médicament, peuvent aider les patients à se calmer et améliorer rapidement leur santé dans des situations stressantes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent faire des études plus larges pour savoir si c'est la VR, la musique, ou les deux ensemble qui fonctionnent le mieux. Ils prévoient aussi de tester si laisser les patients choisir leur musique aide encore plus.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Combiner des scènes naturelles virtuelles avec de la musique classique peut rapidement réduire l'hypertension et l'anxiété chez les patients hospitalisés, en complément des médicaments.
articles.personality_title_es: La realidad virtual y la música clásica ayudan a bajar la presión arterial alta en hospitales
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La presión arterial alta puede ser peligrosa y es común en las salas de emergencia. El tratamiento habitual incluye medicamentos, pero el estrés y la ansiedad pueden empeorarla al estrechar los vasos sanguíneos.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores en Turquía probaron una nueva forma de ayudar a pacientes con presión arterial muy alta. También redujeron más su ansiedad. Esto indica que métodos simples sin medicinas pueden ayudar a calmar a los pacientes y mejorar su salud rápido en situaciones estresantes.

**Resumen en una frase** – Combinar escenas naturales virtuales con música clásica puede reducir rápidamente la presión arterial alta y la ansiedad en pacientes hospitalizados junto con el tratamiento médico.

articles.title: How book clubs and bedtime stories protect and build healthier brains
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If the book on your nightstand has been gathering dust, here’s your reason to finally open it. A new review from Cambridge University researchers finds that reading for pleasure, whether that’s a worn paperback or the latest romantasy on your e-reader, is linked to better memory and attention, fewer […]
The post How book clubs and bedtime stories protect and build healthier brains first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

If the book on your nightstand has been gathering dust, here’s your reason to finally open it. A new review from Cambridge University researchers finds that reading for pleasure, whether that’s a worn paperback or the latest romantasy on your e-reader, is linked to better memory and attention, fewer mental health struggles, and a meaningfully lower risk of dementia.

The findings hold across all age groups. You don’t need to have been a voracious childhood reader to benefit, and the habits you build now can pay off well into your later years.

The benefits start early and don’t stop

The Cambridge review drew on multiple studies to trace the cognitive and emotional effects of recreational reading. People who read for pleasure showed stronger attention and memory, lower stress, and a more tolerant outlook toward different perspectives.

“Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our wellbeing,” said Barbara Sahakian, professor at Cambridge and the review’s corresponding author. “It’s something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it’s never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age.”

The findings were especially strong for older adults. Leisure activities that engage the brain are consistently tied to slower cognitive decline and a lower risk of dementia, and reading is one of the most accessible on that list. The researchers call it “an accessible and low-cost protective factor across the lifespan,” which is about as practical a case for picking up a book as you’re going to find.

Starting young helps, but it’s never too late

Despite the growing evidence, reading rates among young people have been falling. The latest PISA 2025 report, which evaluates 15-year-olds across participating countries, shows a global drop in reading performance. Researchers linked the decline to less recreational reading and more digital distraction.

In the UK, data from the National Literacy Trust found that only 36 percent of young people aged 8 to 18 said they enjoyed reading in their free time in the most recent survey, down from nearly 59 percent in 2016.

Co-author Christelle Langley said the key is finding something kids will actually want to read, even if that means starting with a tie-in to a show they love or a game they play. Getting them into the habit matters more than what they’re reading. “Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels,” she said.

Why book clubs do more than you’d think

Reading in a group turned out to be better for the brain than reading alone. Being part of a book club was associated with even greater cognitive benefits, largely because of the social connection it creates.

“They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia,” Sahakian said. “While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they’re perfect for older people who may be not so mobile.”

For anyone who has trouble making it to an exercise class or out to social events regularly, a reading group is something most people can take part in regardless of physical ability. For older adults especially, that matters.

What we still don’t know

The review doesn’t fully explain the brain mechanisms behind all of this, and the researchers acknowledge more work is needed. The precise pathways are still being mapped.

What the review does point to clearly is that reading interventions work, and that policies backing early reading habits through schools, libraries, and community programs could help offset some of the developmental effects of poverty. Reading is low-cost, widely available, and, according to this research, something the brain genuinely benefits from at every stage of life. That’s a hard combination to argue with.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

It highlights accessible, low-cost cognitive and emotional benefits with broad societal implications, especially for children and older adults. The article also emphasizes the social benefits of book clubs, adding meaningful context and actionable insights.
articles.personality_title: Reading for pleasure boosts brain health at any age
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Researchers from Cambridge University reviewed many studies to understand how reading for fun affects our brains. They wanted to see if enjoying books helps people think better and feel healthier.

**What happened** – The review found that reading for pleasure improves memory and attention, reduces stress and mental health problems, and lowers the chance of dementia. These benefits happen to people of all ages, from children to older adults. The study also showed that joining book clubs adds extra brain benefits because of social interaction.

**Impact** – This is important because reading is a simple, low-cost activity that anyone can do. It helps keep the brain sharp and supports emotional well-being. The findings suggest that even starting to read later in life can protect against mental decline. Book clubs help reduce loneliness, which is linked to better brain health, especially for older people.

**What's next step** – The researchers want to learn more about how reading affects the brain’s inner workings. They also suggest schools, libraries, and communities encourage reading from a young age to build healthy brain habits. Finding ways to make reading fun, like comics or tie-ins to favorite shows, can help kids enjoy it more.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Reading for pleasure is a powerful, easy way to improve brain health and emotional well-being throughout life.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:

articles.personality_title_es: Leer por placer mejora la salud cerebral a cualquier edad
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Cambridge revisaron muchos estudios para entender cómo la lectura por diversión afecta nuestro cerebro. Querían saber si disfrutar los libros ayuda a pensar mejor y sentirse más saludable.

**Qué pasó** – La revisión encontró que leer por placer mejora la memoria y la atención, reduce el estrés y los problemas de salud mental, y baja el riesgo de demencia. Estos beneficios ocurren en todas las edades, desde niños hasta adultos mayores. Además, participar en clubes de lectura aporta beneficios extras por la conexión social.

Empezar a leer incluso en la edad adulta puede proteger contra el deterioro mental. Los clubes de lectura ayudan a reducir la soledad, lo que mejora la salud cerebral, especialmente en personas mayores.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren aprender más sobre cómo la lectura afecta el funcionamiento del cerebro. También sugieren que escuelas, bibliotecas y comunidades fomenten la lectura desde pequeños. Encontrar formas de hacer la lectura divertida, como con cómics o libros relacionados con programas favoritos, puede ayudar a los niños a disfrutarla más.
